conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Roll two dice. How many of the 36 outcomes show **at least one 6**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 6 + 6. The outcome (6, 6) appears in both lists, so a plain sum counts it twice — subtract it once.
That is only (6, 6). "At least one" also includes rolls like (6, 2) and (3, 6) where a single die shows the 6.
That is the count of rolls with **no** 6. It is the complement — the answer is 36 − 25.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: Count what fails: 5 × 5 = 25 rolls have no 6, so 36 − 25 = 11 rolls have at least one.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Flip four coins. How many of the 16 outcomes show **at least one head**?

commonErrors.feedback: That counts only the outcomes with **exactly** one head. "At least one" also allows two, three or four heads.
That is every outcome, but TTTT has no head at all, so it must be excluded — 16 − 1 = 15.
That is half of 16, the count for a single fixed coin landing heads. The event allows *any* of the four coins to be the head.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: Only TTTT fails, so 16 − 1 = 15 outcomes contain at least one head.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Roll three dice (216 equally likely outcomes). How many show **at least one 6**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the count of rolls with **no** 6 — the complement. Subtract it from 216 to get the rolls that do contain a six.
That is 216 × 1/2, which is what you get by adding 1/6 three times. Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
That is 6 × 6, the count for one fixed die showing a 6. The other two dice still have to be accounted for.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: Count the misses: 5³ = 125 rolls have no six, so 216 − 125 = 91 rolls have at least one.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Roll two dice. How many of the 36 outcomes show **at least one 5**?

commonErrors.feedback: Adding the six outcomes from each die counts (5, 5) twice. Subtract that overlap once.
Twenty-five is the number of outcomes with no 5. Subtract it from all 36 outcomes.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: There are 5 × 5 = 25 outcomes with no 5, so 36 − 25 = 11 outcomes have at least one 5.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Flip five coins. How many of the 32 outcomes show **at least one tail**?

commonErrors.feedback: Five counts outcomes with exactly one tail. At least one tail includes all outcomes except HHHHH.
HHHHH has no tail, so one of the 32 outcomes must be excluded.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: Only HHHHH has no tail, so 32 − 1 = 31 outcomes have at least one tail.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: A four-section spinner has one red section. Spin it three times. How many of the 64 outcomes show **at least one red**?

commonErrors.feedback: Twenty-seven counts the outcomes with no red because each spin has three non-red choices.
Adding one-fourth three times counts overlaps more than once. Use the complement instead.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: The no-red outcomes number 3³ = 27, so 64 − 27 = 37 outcomes contain at least one red.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Roll two eight-sided dice. How many of the 64 outcomes show **at least one 8**?

commonErrors.feedback: Adding eight outcomes from each die counts (8, 8) twice. Remove the duplicate once.
Forty-nine counts the outcomes with no 8. Subtract that complement from 64.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: There are 7 × 7 = 49 outcomes with no 8, so 64 − 49 = 15 have at least one 8.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Six independent sensors each report pass or fail. How many of the 64 report patterns show **at least one fail**?

commonErrors.feedback: Six counts patterns with exactly one fail. At least one fail includes every pattern except all-pass.
The all-pass pattern contains no fail, so it must be excluded.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: Only the all-pass pattern has no fail, so 64 − 1 = 63 patterns have at least one fail.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.prompt: Roll two ten-sided dice numbered 0 through 9. How many of the 100 outcomes show **at least one 0**?

commonErrors.feedback: Adding ten outcomes for each die counts (0, 0) twice. Subtract the overlap once.
Eighty-one is the number of outcomes with no 0. Subtract it from 100.

conditional-probability__cpr-at-least-on.fallbackFeedback: There are 9 × 9 = 81 outcomes with no 0, so 100 − 81 = 19 have at least one 0.

conditional-probability__cpr-complement-.prompt: A student is picked at random. Which pair of events are complements?

options.label: "Bus or sport" and "walks and no sport"
options.feedback: Right — they cover the table with no overlap, so their probabilities must sum to 1: 0.85 + 0.15.

options.label: "Bus or sport" and "bus and sport"
options.feedback: These overlap heavily — the 40 in the crossing cell satisfy both descriptions. Complements can share no one.

options.label: "Takes the bus" and "plays a sport"
options.feedback: A student can do both (40 do) and a student can do neither (30 do). Complements allow neither case.

options.label: "Walks" and "plays no sport"
options.feedback: These two overlap in the 30 walkers with no sport, so they are not complements. Their probabilities sum to 0.95, not 1.

conditional-probability__cpr-complement-.prompt: P(neither takes the bus nor plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the union itself — the students who DO satisfy at least one event. "Neither" is what is left over: 1 − 0.85.
That is P(walks). Walking alone is not enough — the 70 walkers who play a sport still satisfy the "sport" half.
That is P(no sport), the whole column. The 60 bus riders inside it are still in the union via the bus row.

conditional-probability__cpr-complement-.fallbackFeedback: The single unshaded cell holds 30 students: 30/200 = 0.15 = 1 − 0.85.

conditional-probability__cpr-complement-.prompt: Of 150 phones, 90 have a case, 60 have a screen protector, and 40 have both. Find **P(neither)** as a decimal, rounded to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the union, 110/150 — the phones with at least one accessory. "Neither" is the leftover: 1 − 0.733.
That is 80/150, which comes from subtracting the 40 overlap twice. It is added twice by 90 + 60, so it comes off exactly once.
That comes from 90 + 60 = 150, as if every phone had exactly one accessory. But 40 phones have both, so those two counts overlap and the union is only 110.

conditional-probability__cpr-complement-.fallbackFeedback: 90 + 60 − 40 = 110 phones have at least one, so 150 − 110 = 40 have neither: 40/150 ≈ 0.267.

conditional-probability__cpr-complement_.prompt: Three coins are flipped. What is the complement of "at least one head"?

options.label: No heads at all (TTT)
options.feedback: Right — the only way to miss "one or more heads" is to get zero of them.

options.label: At least one tail
options.feedback: That is not an opposite: HHT has at least one head *and* at least one tail, so both events happen together. Complements can never overlap.

options.label: Exactly one head
options.feedback: Exactly one head is *inside* "at least one head", not opposite to it. The complement must contain none of A's outcomes.

options.label: All heads (HHH)
options.feedback: HHH is the most extreme case of "at least one head", so it belongs to the event itself, not to its complement.

conditional-probability__cpr-conditional.prompt: Each statement uses the same 40 students. Match it to its fraction.

left.label: Given they take the bus, they play a sport
Given they play a sport, they take the bus
They take the bus and play a sport

pairErrors.feedback: Being told they ride the bus makes the 100 bus riders the world, so the denominator is 100, not 110.
An "and" statement conditions on nothing — its denominator is everybody: 200.

conditional-probability__cpr-conditional.missFeedback: Find the word "given". Whatever follows it is the denominator; with no "given", the denominator is all 200.
conditional-probability__cpr-conditional.successFeedback: Three statements, one numerator, three denominators — that is the whole idea of conditioning.

conditional-probability__cpr-conditional.prompt: P(plays a sport | takes the bus). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the joint probability 40/200 — dividing by everyone. The condition already cut the world down to the 100 bus riders.
That is 40/110, which conditions on **sport** instead. You were told the travel method, so the sport column is not the surviving world.
That is P(sport) for the whole school. The point of conditioning is that the bus riders need not match the school average.

conditional-probability__cpr-conditional.fallbackFeedback: Of the 100 bus riders, 40 play a sport: 0.40.

conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.prompt: One card is drawn. Classify each pair of events.

items.label: the card is a heart · the card is a spade
items.feedback: A card has one suit, so these cannot both happen. P(spade | heart) = 0, far from P(spade) = 1/4.

items.label: the card is a heart · the card is a queen
items.feedback: The queen of hearts exists, and P(queen | heart) = 1/13 = P(queen). They overlap at exactly the product rate.

items.label: the card is red · the card is a club
items.feedback: Clubs are black, so no card is both. Learning it is red makes 'club' impossible.

items.label: the card is red · the card is an ace
items.feedback: P(ace | red) = 2/26 = 1/13 = P(ace). Red aces exist, and they occur at exactly the product rate.

conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.missFeedback: Ask first: can one card satisfy both? If it cannot, they are exclusive. If it can, compare P(A | B) with P(A).
conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.successFeedback: Suit-vs-suit and colour-vs-suit collide; suit-vs-rank never does — and rank is independent of suit.

conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.prompt: Match each property to the shortcut it licenses.

right.label: No shortcut — use P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A|B)

pairErrors.feedback: Exclusive events have P(A ∩ B) = 0, while P(A) × P(B) is positive — so that is the one product formula exclusivity forbids.
Independent events usually overlap, so plain addition double-counts the overlap. Independence licenses the AND shortcut, not the OR one.

conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.missFeedback: Exclusive simplifies OR (nothing to subtract). Independent simplifies AND (no conditional needed).
conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.successFeedback: One property per shortcut — and with neither property you fall back on the general multiplication rule.

conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.prompt: One die. A = "even", B = "shows a 5". These are mutually exclusive. Are they independent?

options.label: Dependent — knowing it is a 5 drops P(even) from 1/2 to 0.
options.feedback: Right — exclusivity is the strongest dependence there is: one event rules the other out completely.

options.label: Independent — they never interfere with each other.
options.feedback: They interfere as much as two events possibly can. Learning that A happened makes B impossible, which is the opposite of leaving it unchanged.

options.label: Independent — P(A and B) = 0 = P(A) × P(B).
options.feedback: The joint is 0, but the product is 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12, not 0. The product test fails.

options.label: Both, since the two ideas mean the same thing.
options.feedback: They are different ideas — and for events with non-zero probability, they cannot both hold.

conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3, and A and B are **mutually exclusive**. Find P(A | B).

commonErrors.feedback: That is P(A) — the answer if the events were *independent*. Exclusive is the opposite: B happening makes A impossible.
That is 0.5 × 0.3, the product an independence assumption would give for the joint. But exclusivity forces the joint to 0.
That is 0.5 + 0.3 = P(A ∪ B), which is the one thing exclusivity *does* let you compute by adding. The conditional is 0.

conditional-probability__cpr-indep-vs-di.fallbackFeedback: Exclusive ⇒ P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A | B) = 0/0.3 = 0.

conditional-probability__cpr-joint-prob_.prompt: Match each probability to the count above 200.

pairErrors.feedback: 70 is the walkers who play — one inner cell. P(bus) is the whole bus row: 40 + 60 = 100.
100 is a row total (bus). The no-sport column totals 60 + 30 = 90.

conditional-probability__cpr-joint-prob_.missFeedback: Rows total 100 and 100; columns total 110 and 90; inner cells are 40, 60, 70, 30.
conditional-probability__cpr-joint-prob_.successFeedback: Two edges and one cell — you can now read any joint or marginal probability straight off the table.

conditional-probability__cpr-joint-prob_.prompt: P(takes the bus **and** plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 40/100 — you divided by the bus row instead of the whole group. A joint probability always divides by the grand total, 200.
That is 40/110 — dividing by the sport column. For a joint probability the denominator is everyone: 200.
That is P(bus), the whole row. The question asks for students who are in the bus row AND the sport column: the single cell where they cross.

conditional-probability__cpr-joint-prob_.prompt: You are told only this: 200 students, 90 play no sport, 30 of those 90 walk, and 100 take the bus. Find **P(takes the bus and plays no sport)**.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 60/90 — dividing by the no-sport column. That is a conditional probability; a joint one divides by all 200.
That is 90/200, the marginal P(no sport). The question asks for the bus riders inside that column, which is 90 − 30 = 60.
That is 30/200 — the walkers with no sport. The bus riders in that column are the other 60.

conditional-probability__cpr-joint-prob_.fallbackFeedback: 90 − 30 = 60 bus riders play no sport, so 60/200 = 0.30.

conditional-probability__cpr-marginal-pr.prompt: Which of these is a **marginal** probability?

options.label: P(walks) = 100/200
options.feedback: Right — it uses a whole edge total and says nothing about sport, so one question has been collapsed away.

options.label: P(walks and no sport) = 30/200
options.feedback: Both questions are pinned down, so this is one inner cell: a joint probability.

options.label: P(bus and sport) = 40/200
options.feedback: The "and" is the giveaway — two questions answered at once means one inner cell, which is joint.

options.label: P(sport, among bus riders) = 40/100
options.feedback: That divides by 100, not 200 — it is a conditional probability, restricted to the bus row. That is the next chapter.

conditional-probability__cpr-marginal-pr.prompt: P(plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the joint cell 40/200 — bus riders who play a sport. The marginal also counts the 70 walkers who play.
That is 70/200, the walkers who play. Add the 40 bus riders who play as well: 110 of 200.
That is 90/200 — the *no sport* column. The two columns are complements, so a slip here flips the event.

conditional-probability__cpr-marginal-pr.fallbackFeedback: Sum the whole sport column: 40 + 70 = 110, so 110/200 = 0.55.

conditional-probability__cpr-multiplicat.prompt: When can you compute P(A and B) as simply P(A) × P(B)?

options.label: When knowing A leaves the chance of B unchanged.
options.feedback: Right — then P(B | A) = P(B), and the general rule collapses to the product of marginals. That condition has a name, coming next chapter.

options.label: Always — that is what "and" means.
options.feedback: The bus students showed otherwise: 0.50 × 0.55 = 0.275, but the true joint is 0.20. Knowing they ride the bus changes their sport rate.

options.label: Whenever A and B cannot both happen.
options.feedback: If they cannot both happen, P(A and B) is 0, and the product of two positive marginals certainly is not 0.

options.label: Whenever A and B have the same probability.
options.feedback: Equal probabilities say nothing about whether one event informs the other. What matters is whether P(B | A) equals P(B).

conditional-probability__cpr-mutually-ex.prompt: One card is drawn from cards 1–20. Which pair of events is mutually exclusive?

options.label: "the number is even" and "the number is odd"
options.feedback: Right — no card is both, so the events share zero outcomes and cannot happen together.

options.label: "the number is even" and "the number is a multiple of 5"
options.feedback: Cards 10 and 20 are both even and multiples of 5, so the events overlap — exclusivity needs zero shared outcomes.

options.label: "the number is greater than 15" and "the number is a multiple of 3"
options.feedback: Card 18 satisfies both at once, so these events can co-occur; one shared outcome is enough to break exclusivity.

options.label: "the number is prime" and "the number is odd"
options.feedback: Most primes here are odd — 3, 5, 7, 11 … — so the events overlap heavily. Sharing outcomes is the opposite of exclusive.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: In a class of 30, 18 play a sport, 12 play an instrument, and 7 do both. How many do **at least one**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 18 + 12 with the 7 double-counted, which happens to hit the class size — a coincidence, not an answer. Subtract the overlap: 30 − 7 = 23.
That is the number doing **both**. "At least one" includes the sport-only and instrument-only students too.
That looks like 30 − 5. The students doing neither are not given; they come *out* of the answer, they do not set it.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: These events are not exclusive: 18 + 12 counts the 7 doubles twice, so at least one = 18 + 12 − 7 = 23.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: 40 people are surveyed: 25 like coffee, 18 like tea, 5 like neither. How many like **both**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 43 − 40 — you subtracted the whole group instead of the group that likes at least one. Five people like neither, so only 35 are inside the circles.
That is 25 + 18, the double-counted total. The people who like both were counted in each number, so this sum overshoots.
That is the number who like **neither** — a given, not the answer. Use it to find that 35 like at least one, then compare with 25 + 18.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: 35 like at least one (40 − 5). Since 25 + 18 = 43 counts the both-likers twice, both = 43 − 35 = 8.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 36 students, 22 joined art club, 17 joined coding club, and 9 joined both. How many joined **at least one** club?

commonErrors.feedback: That adds both club counts but counts the 9 students in both clubs twice. Subtract the overlap once.
That is only the overlap. At least one club also includes students who joined just art or just coding.
That is the art-only count, 22 − 9. The question asks for everyone in either club, including the overlap.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: Add the two club counts, then remove the duplicated overlap once: 22 + 17 − 9 = 30.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 48 visitors, 31 entered the gallery, 24 joined a workshop, and 11 did neither. How many did **both**?

commonErrors.feedback: That subtracts the full group from 31 + 24. First remove the 11 visitors who did neither to find the union.
That is 31 + 24, where visitors who did both are counted twice. Compare it with the 37 who did at least one.
That is the number who did neither. Use it to find that 37 visitors did at least one activity.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: First, 48 − 11 = 37 did at least one. Then 31 + 24 − 37 = 18 did both.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 50 children, 28 can swim, 21 can cycle, and 8 can do both. How many can do **at least one** activity?

commonErrors.feedback: That adds 28 + 21 but counts the 8 children who can do both twice. Subtract the overlap once.
That is only the overlap. At least one activity includes the swim-only and cycle-only groups as well.
That is the swim-only count, 28 − 8. The union must also include the cycle-only group and the overlap.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: Use inclusion–exclusion: 28 + 21 − 8 = 41 children can do at least one activity.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 60 households, 35 use streaming, 27 use cable, and 9 use neither. How many use **both**?

commonErrors.feedback: That compares 35 + 27 with all 60 households. The 9 using neither must be removed before finding the overlap.
That is the double-counted sum 35 + 27. The overlap is the amount by which that sum exceeds the union of 51.
That is the number using neither service. It helps find the union, but it is not the overlap.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: First, 60 − 9 = 51 use at least one service. Then 35 + 27 − 51 = 11 use both.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 42 volunteers, 26 helped in the garden, 19 helped in the kitchen, and 10 helped in both. How many helped in **at least one** place?

commonErrors.feedback: That adds both groups but counts the 10 volunteers who helped in both places twice. Subtract the overlap once.
That is only the overlap. At least one place includes every garden-only and kitchen-only volunteer too.
That is the garden-only count, 26 − 10. The question asks for the full union of the two groups.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: Count the union once: 26 + 19 − 10 = 35 volunteers helped in at least one place.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 72 travellers, 44 used the train, 37 used the bus, and 15 used neither. How many used **both**?

commonErrors.feedback: That subtracts all 72 travellers from 44 + 37. First remove the 15 who used neither to find the union.
That is 44 + 37, where travellers who used both are counted twice. Compare it with the union of 57.
That is the number who used neither. It determines the union but is not the number who used both.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: First, 72 − 15 = 57 used at least one. Then 44 + 37 − 57 = 24 used both.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 64 readers, 39 chose fiction, 28 chose nonfiction, and 12 chose both. How many chose **at least one** type?

commonErrors.feedback: That adds 39 + 28 but counts the 12 readers who chose both types twice. Remove that duplicate count once.
That is only the overlap. At least one type includes readers who chose exactly one type as well.
That is the fiction-only count, 39 − 12. The union also includes nonfiction-only readers and the overlap.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: Use inclusion–exclusion: 39 + 28 − 12 = 55 readers chose at least one type.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.prompt: Of 90 attendees, 52 joined the morning session, 46 joined the afternoon session, and 14 joined neither. How many joined **both** sessions?

commonErrors.feedback: That compares 52 + 46 with all 90 attendees. First remove the 14 who joined neither to find the union.
That is the sum of the two session counts, where attendees in both sessions are counted twice.
That is the number who joined neither session. It helps find the union but does not equal the overlap.

conditional-probability__cpr-overlap-cou.fallbackFeedback: First, 90 − 14 = 76 joined at least one session. Then 52 + 46 − 76 = 22 joined both.

conditional-probability__cpr-reversal-er.prompt: "Of the students who walk, 70% play a sport." Which probability is that?

options.label: P(plays a sport | walks) = 70/100
options.feedback: Right — the walkers are the group being divided by, so they sit under the line.

options.label: P(walks | plays a sport) = 70/110
options.feedback: That reverses the sentence. It would read "of the students who play a sport, 64% walk" — a true statement, but a different one.

options.label: P(walks and plays a sport) = 70/200
options.feedback: That is the joint probability, 0.35 — the share of the *whole school*. The sentence restricts attention to walkers first.

options.label: P(walks) = 100/200
options.feedback: That is the condition on its own. The 70% describes what happens *inside* that group.

conditional-probability__cpr-reversal-er.prompt: P(takes the bus | plays a sport). Give a decimal, to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 40/100 = P(sport | bus) — the reverse conditional. Here you are told the sport, so you divide by the 110 who play, not the 100 who ride.
That is the joint 40/200. A conditional divides by its condition, and the condition here contains 110 students.
That is P(bus) across the whole school. Being told the student plays a sport should move that number — it lands at 40/110 ≈ 0.364.

conditional-probability__cpr-reversal-er.fallbackFeedback: Of the 110 who play a sport, 40 take the bus: 40/110 ≈ 0.364.

conditional-probability__cpr-reversal-er.prompt: P(walks | plays no sport). Give a decimal, to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 30/100 = P(no sport | walks) — the reversed conditional. You were told about sport, so the 90 non-players are the denominator, not the 100 walkers.
That is the joint 30/200. Conditioning on "no sport" shrinks the world to 90 students, so the denominator cannot still be 200.
That is P(no sport) = 90/200, the condition itself. The question asks what fraction of that group walks.

conditional-probability__cpr-reversal-er.fallbackFeedback: The no-sport column holds 90 students, 30 of whom walk: 30/90 ≈ 0.333.

conditional-probability__cpr-table-union.prompt: Why do we subtract the 40 when we add the bus row (100) to the sport column (110)?

options.label: Because they sit in both the row and the column.
options.feedback: Exactly — sitting in both means they're counted twice: 100 + 110 = 210, which overshoots the 170 shaded students by precisely those 40.

options.label: Because those 40 students belong to neither event.
options.feedback: The 40 belong to BOTH events, which is why they are double-counted. The students who belong to neither are the 30 in the last cell.

options.label: To make the probability come out under 1.
options.feedback: Staying under 1 is a symptom, not the reason. The subtraction exists because a double-counted student must be counted once.

options.label: Because the row and the column have different totals.
options.feedback: Unequal totals are fine — the row and column here happen to be 100 and 110. The correction is about the shared cell, not the sizes.

conditional-probability__cpr-table-union.prompt: P(takes the bus **or** plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 0.50 + 0.55 with nothing subtracted — and a probability above 1 is the tell. The 40 in the crossing cell got counted twice.
That is the joint cell, P(bus and sport). "Or" is the larger event: it also holds for the 60 bus riders with no sport and the 70 walkers who play.
That is P(sport) alone. The 60 bus riders who play no sport still satisfy "bus or sport".

conditional-probability__cpr-table-union.fallbackFeedback: 0.50 + 0.55 − 0.20 = 0.85, which matches the 170 shaded students out of 200.
